To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the water status of leaves and stems is affected differently by soil moisture and microclimate.

(i) stem and leaf water status of young oak trees are highly responsive to short- and long-term variations in soil moisture and atmospheric VPD, and (ii) the diurnal stem water variations are delayed with respect to the diurnal leaf turgor fluctuations.
stem radius changes and leaf patch pressure variations are strongly dependent on microclimate (solar radiation, vapour pressure deficit) and soil water availability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new tools to monitor stem and leaf water relations in trees.
the development and application of the LPCP probe for measuring leaf turgor and the analysis of the effects of microclimate and water stress on tree water relations.

the diurnal regulation of water relations in young oaks, and the effects of soil moisture and microclimate on the regulation of stem water content and leaf turgors in the context of hydraulic integration.

stem water and leaf turgor variations in young oak are mainly driven by VPD and SWC and that the diurnal patterns are mainly driven by solar radiation.
ΔW and P is a function of VPD, SWC, soil water uptake, and hydraulic conductivity of the stem and leaves, but the exact mechanisms are not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diurnal patterns of ΔW and turgor are determined by the interplay of environmental and physiological processes, and their interactions with tree water status.

dendrometers and LPCP probes provide complementary information on tree water relations, and that the combination of both sensors allows for an improved assessment of tree water status in response to microclimate and soil water availability.
